title: The Hasmoneans
hook: the rebels became kings, and later rabbis were wary of their power

segments.voice: Yesterday, weeds in the Temple courtyards, a new altar, eight days of gladness. Your line was rededicate. What did you give back its purpose? Today, a harder question: what happens to rebels after they win? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

Words on brass. Near the end of the first book of Maccabees, the people of Jerusalem write their thanks on tablets of brass and set them up on pillars on Mount Zion. The tablets honor Simon, a son of Mattathias. The book is glowing about his years: the land had peace, it says, and every man sat under his own vine and his own fig tree, with no one to make him afraid. So the people make Simon their leader and their high priest. But they add a condition, written right into the decree: until a faithful prophet should arise. The family of Mattathias, the Hasmoneans, now holds the sword, the Temple and the government. The question the next chapters of Jewish history ask is what that much power does to a family of heroes.
screen: `THANKS WRITTEN ON BRASS.` → `EVERY MAN UNDER HIS FIG TREE.` → `UNTIL A FAITHFUL PROPHET ARISES.`

segments.voice: Years later. In the Talmud, the Hasmonean ruler is now called King Yannai, and he wears two crowns: the crown of a king and the crown of the high priest. Tractate Kiddushin tells a tense story. Yannai comes home from a victory and throws a feast for the sages of Israel. At the table, one guest stirs him up, telling him the sages resent him. Then an elder named Yehudah ben Gedidyah speaks up, with the whole room listening: King Yannai, let the crown of kingship be enough for you. Leave the crown of priesthood to the descendants of Aaron. The story says Yannai, furious, turns on the sages and kills them, and the world is left desolate of Torah until Shimon ben Shetach restores it. Remember who this family was. Mattathias's sons risked everything so that no king could force his will on the Temple. Their descendants end up as kings the sages feared. Some readers think that's why, when the Talmud asks what Hanukkah is, it answers with a jar of oil and the lights, not a throne. And another passage, in tractate Berakhot, tells of a high priest named Yochanan who served faithfully for many years and changed at the end. The Talmud ties it to Hillel's warning from Pirkei Avot: do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. Heroes can change. The power that rescues can become the power that crushes, sometimes within one family.
screen: `TWO CROWNS ON ONE HEAD.` · `LET THE KINGSHIP BE ENOUGH.` · `OIL AND LIGHTS, NOT A THRONE.` · then, large: `DO NOT TRUST IN YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to watch what power does to heroes, starting close to home. Settle and breathe. Think of a moment you had a little power: a promotion, being the oldest sibling, being the one who knew the password, being right in an argument. Did you use it the way you would have wanted when you had less? No need to judge. Just look honestly. Then think of one person you admire who now holds power, and wish them the wisdom of Yehudah ben Gedidyah's line: let one crown be enough. If you pray, you can use words from your tradition to ask to stay faithful to who you were. The bell holds the time.
The Hasmoneans. The family of Mattathias, who rescued the Temple, and whose descendants became kings the rabbis were wary of. Today's word.
Your line: heroes can change. Today, when you have a little power over someone, use it the way you'd want it used on you. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Students of Pirkei Avot learn Hillel's warning, do not trust in yourself until the day of your death, and the Talmud's stories of King Yannai and of Yochanan the high priest are studied in tractates Kiddushin and Berakhot.

fork.setup: you're a sage at King Yannai's feast. he wears both crowns, king and high priest. the room is watching. what do you say?
options: let the crown of kingship be enough; leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants.
fork.reveal: in tractate Kiddushin, Yehudah ben Gedidyah says it out loud. the story says Yannai turns on the sages in his anger.

original.note: Hebrew: Hasmonean, the family name of Mattathias and his descendants, used in the Hanukkah prayer Al HaNissim.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Maccabees were heroes, full stop.
what it means: the rescuers founded a dynasty, and later generations held power the rabbis were wary of.
what a scholar hears: 1 Maccabees 14 limits Simon's office until a faithful prophet arises; Kiddushin 66a tells of King Yannai and the sages; Berakhot 29a cites Avot 2:4.

notes: 1 Maccabees 14 paraphrased: peace under Simon, 'every man under his vine and his fig tree' (14:12, echoing Micah 4:4); brass tablets on pillars on Mount Zion (14:26–27, 14:48); Simon governor and high priest 'for ever, until there should arise a faithful prophet' (14:41).

Kiddushin 66a paraphrased (Yannai, Elazar ben Po'ira, Yehudah ben Gedidyah, the killing of the sages, Shimon ben Shetach). Please confirm; the guest 'stirs him up' compresses Elazar ben Po'ira's role.

Berakhot 29a: Yochanan the High Priest served many years and in the end became a Sadducee; the script says only that he 'changed at the end' (the Sadducees are introduced tomorrow). Some identify him with John Hyrcanus; not claimed here.
The link between the rabbis' wariness and Shabbat 21b's focus on the oil is framed as 'some readers think'; please check.
Claims rule: no dates or generation counts given.
Editor: hook now matches the KJV 'tables of brass'; cut 'the last surviving son' (not in the cited chapter 14); cut a stock line about villains and people.
